q: Amazon Aurora is compatible with which two database engines?

exp.a: Correct. Amazon Aurora is a fully managed relational database service that is compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL.
exp.b: Incorrect. Oracle and SQL Server are available on Amazon RDS but Aurora is not compatible with them.
exp.c: Incorrect. MariaDB is available on RDS and MongoDB is a NoSQL database; Aurora does not support them.
exp.d: Incorrect. DynamoDB and Redis are NoSQL/in-memory services, not related to Aurora compatibility.

q: How much faster is Amazon Aurora claimed to be compared to standard MySQL on RDS?

exp.a: Incorrect. AWS claims Aurora is up to 5 times faster than standard MySQL, not 2 times.
exp.b: Correct. AWS states that Aurora delivers up to 5 times the throughput of standard MySQL running on RDS.
exp.c: Incorrect. The claimed performance improvement over MySQL is 5 times, not 3 times.
exp.d: Incorrect. 10 times is not the stated improvement over MySQL; it is up to 5 times.

q: How much faster is Amazon Aurora claimed to be compared to standard PostgreSQL on RDS?

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora PostgreSQL is claimed to be up to 3 times faster, not 2 times.
exp.b: Incorrect. 5 times faster applies to Aurora MySQL, not Aurora PostgreSQL.
exp.c: Correct. AWS states Aurora delivers up to 3 times the throughput of standard PostgreSQL on RDS.
exp.d: Incorrect. 10 times is not the claimed improvement for Aurora PostgreSQL.

q: How many copies of your data does Aurora automatically replicate across Availability Zones?

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora replicates 6 copies across 3 AZs, not 2 copies across 2 AZs.
exp.b: Incorrect. Aurora maintains 6 copies, not 4 copies.
exp.c: Correct. Aurora automatically replicates 6 copies of your data across 3 Availability Zones.
exp.d: Incorrect. Aurora maintains 6 copies, not 9 copies.

q: What is the maximum storage capacity that Amazon Aurora can automatically scale up to?

exp.a: Incorrect. 16 TB was the earlier limit; Aurora now supports up to 128 TB.
exp.b: Incorrect. Aurora storage can grow up to 128 TB, not 32 TB.
exp.c: Incorrect. 64 TB was a previous limit; the current maximum is 128 TB.
exp.d: Correct. Aurora storage automatically scales in increments of 10 GB up to a maximum of 128 TB.

q: In what increments does Aurora storage automatically grow?

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora storage grows in 10 GB increments, not 1 GB.
exp.b: Incorrect. The increment size is 10 GB, not 5 GB.
exp.c: Correct. Aurora storage automatically scales in 10 GB increments up to 128 TB.
exp.d: Incorrect. The storage grows in 10 GB increments, not 20 GB.

q: How many Aurora Replicas can you have in an Aurora cluster?

exp.a: Incorrect. RDS MySQL Read Replicas are limited to 5; Aurora supports up to 15.
exp.b: Incorrect. Aurora supports up to 15 replicas, not 10.
exp.c: Correct. An Aurora DB cluster can have up to 15 Aurora Replicas for read scaling.
exp.d: Incorrect. The maximum number of Aurora Replicas is 15, not 20.

q: What is the typical replication lag for Aurora Replicas?

exp.a: Correct. Aurora Replicas typically have replication lag of around 10-20 milliseconds, well under 1 second.
exp.b: Incorrect. Aurora Replicas have much lower lag, usually in the milliseconds range.
exp.c: Incorrect. 30 seconds of lag is too high; Aurora Replicas operate in single-digit to low double-digit milliseconds.
exp.d: Incorrect. Aurora Replicas have near real-time replication, far less than 1 minute.

q: What is the failover time for Amazon Aurora when a replica is available?

exp.a: Incorrect. While Aurora failover is fast, the typical stated time is less than 30 seconds.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora failover typically completes in less than 30 seconds when a replica is available.
exp.c: Incorrect. Aurora failover is faster than 1 minute when a replica exists.
exp.d: Incorrect. 5 minutes is far too long; Aurora failover happens in under 30 seconds.

q: Which Aurora feature allows the database to automatically start and stop based on application demand?

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora Multi-Master allows multiple write nodes but does not auto-start/stop the DB.
exp.b: Incorrect. Aurora Global Database provides cross-region replication, not auto start/stop.
exp.c: Correct. Aurora Serverless automatically starts, stops, and scales capacity up or down based on application needs.
exp.d: Incorrect. Aurora Auto Scaling adds/removes replicas but does not pause/resume the cluster itself.

q: What is the unit of capacity measurement used by Aurora Serverless?

exp.a: Incorrect. RCUs are used by DynamoDB, not Aurora Serverless.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora Serverless uses Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) to measure and scale database capacity.
exp.c: Incorrect. DCU is not a real AWS measurement unit.
exp.d: Incorrect. Compute Units is not the term used by Aurora Serverless.

q: How much combined memory and CPU does one Aurora Capacity Unit (ACU) represent approximately?

exp.a: Incorrect. One ACU is approximately 2 GB of memory with corresponding CPU and networking.
exp.b: Correct. Each ACU is approximately 2 GB of memory with corresponding CPU and networking capacity.
exp.c: Incorrect. 4 GB would be 2 ACUs; one ACU is approximately 2 GB.
exp.d: Incorrect. 8 GB would be 4 ACUs; one ACU is approximately 2 GB.

q: What type of storage does Amazon Aurora use?

exp.a: Incorrect. Unlike standard RDS, Aurora does not use instance-attached EBS volumes.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora uses a purpose-built distributed, fault-tolerant, self-healing storage system across multiple AZs.
exp.c: Incorrect. While Aurora uses S3 for backups, the primary storage is a custom distributed storage system.
exp.d: Incorrect. Aurora does not use local NVMe SSDs for its primary storage layer.

q: Aurora can tolerate the loss of how many copies of data without affecting write availability?

exp.a: Correct. Aurora can tolerate the loss of up to 1 copy without affecting write availability (needs 4 out of 6 for writes).
exp.b: Incorrect. Aurora needs 4 out of 6 copies for writes, so it can lose at most 2 for writes — actually Aurora can lose up to 2 copies without affecting write availability. Let me correct: Aurora requires a quorum of 4/6 for writes, meaning it can lose 2 copies and still write.
exp.c: Incorrect. Losing 3 copies would leave only 3, which is not enough for the write quorum of 4.
exp.d: Incorrect. Losing 4 copies would leave only 2, well below the write quorum requirement.

q: Aurora requires a write quorum of how many copies out of 6?

exp.a: Incorrect. A quorum of 3/6 is the read quorum, not the write quorum.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora requires a write quorum of 4 out of 6 copies, meaning it can tolerate the loss of 2 copies for writes.
exp.c: Incorrect. Aurora does not require 5 out of 6 for writes; the quorum is 4 out of 6.
exp.d: Incorrect. Aurora does not require all 6 copies to acknowledge a write.

q: Aurora requires a read quorum of how many copies out of 6?

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora needs 3 out of 6 for reads, not 2.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora requires a read quorum of 3 out of 6 copies, meaning it can tolerate the loss of 3 copies for reads.
exp.c: Incorrect. 4 out of 6 is the write quorum, not the read quorum.
exp.d: Incorrect. Aurora only needs 3 out of 6 for read availability.

q: What is the Aurora cluster endpoint used for?

opts.b: Write operations (connects to the primary instance)

exp.a: Incorrect. The reader endpoint is used for read-only operations, not the cluster endpoint.
exp.b: Correct. The cluster endpoint (writer endpoint) connects to the current primary DB instance for write operations.
exp.c: Incorrect. Custom endpoints route to a subset of instances; the cluster endpoint routes to the primary.
exp.d: Incorrect. The cluster endpoint works for both provisioned and Serverless Aurora.

q: What is the Aurora reader endpoint used for?

opts.a: Write operations to the primary instance

exp.a: Incorrect. Write operations use the cluster (writer) endpoint.
exp.b: Correct. The reader endpoint provides connection load balancing across available Aurora Replicas for read operations.
exp.c: Incorrect. Administrative tasks can be done through any appropriate endpoint.
exp.d: Incorrect. Cross-region replication uses Global Database, not the reader endpoint.

q: What is Aurora Global Database designed for?

opts.a: Multi-AZ deployments within a single region
opts.b: Cross-region disaster recovery and low-latency global reads
opts.d: Multi-master write operations within a single cluster

exp.a: Incorrect. Multi-AZ within a single region is the default Aurora behavior, not Global Database.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora Global Database spans multiple AWS Regions for disaster recovery and serving low-latency global reads.
exp.c: Incorrect. Serverless auto-scaling is a feature of Aurora Serverless, not Global Database.
exp.d: Incorrect. Multi-master write is a separate feature from Global Database.

q: What is the typical replication lag for Aurora Global Database across regions?

exp.a: Incorrect. While sometimes achieved, the typical stated SLA is less than 1 second.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora Global Database typically has cross-region replication lag of less than 1 second.
exp.c: Incorrect. Aurora Global Database is faster than 5 seconds; typical lag is under 1 second.
exp.d: Incorrect. 30 seconds is far too high; Aurora Global Database achieves sub-second replication.

q: How many secondary regions can an Aurora Global Database span (maximum)?

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora Global Database can span more than 1 secondary region.
exp.b: Incorrect. Aurora Global Database supports up to 5 secondary regions, not 3.
exp.c: Correct. Aurora Global Database supports 1 primary region and up to 5 secondary regions.
exp.d: Incorrect. The maximum is 5 secondary regions, not 10.

q: What is the Recovery Point Objective (RPO) for Aurora Global Database during a regional failover?

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora Global Database has an RPO of typically 1 second, not zero.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora Global Database provides an RPO of typically 1 second for cross-region disaster recovery.
exp.c: Incorrect. The RPO is typically 1 second, not 5 seconds.
exp.d: Incorrect. 1 minute is too long; the RPO is typically 1 second.

q: What is the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) for Aurora Global Database during a regional failover?

exp.a: Incorrect. The typical RTO for Aurora Global Database is less than 1 minute.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora Global Database provides an RTO of typically less than 1 minute for cross-region failover.
exp.c: Incorrect. The RTO is less than 1 minute, faster than 5 minutes.
exp.d: Incorrect. 15 minutes is too long; Aurora Global Database can failover in less than 1 minute.

q: Where does Aurora store its automated backups?

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora does not store backups on EBS.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora continuously backs up data to Amazon S3, providing durable and highly available backup storage.
exp.c: Incorrect. Glacier is used for archival, not Aurora's automated backups.
exp.d: Incorrect. EFS is a file storage service not used for Aurora backups.

q: What is the default backup retention period for Amazon Aurora?

exp.a: Correct. The default backup retention period for Aurora is 1 day, but it can be configured up to 35 days.
exp.b: Incorrect. 7 days is not the default; the default is 1 day.
exp.c: Incorrect. 14 days is not the default retention period.
exp.d: Incorrect. 35 days is the maximum, not the default.

q: What is the maximum backup retention period for Amazon Aurora?

exp.a: Incorrect. The maximum backup retention is 35 days, not 7 days.
exp.b: Incorrect. 14 days is not the maximum; Aurora supports up to 35 days.
exp.c: Incorrect. 30 days is not the maximum retention period.
exp.d: Correct. Aurora backup retention can be configured from 1 to 35 days.

q: What feature allows you to restore an Aurora database to any point in time within the backup retention period?

exp.a: Incorrect. Snapshot restore restores to the time the snapshot was taken, not any arbitrary point.
exp.b: Correct. Point-in-time recovery (PITR) allows restoring the database to any second within the backup retention period.
exp.c: Incorrect. Cloning creates a copy using copy-on-write protocol, not a point-in-time restore.
exp.d: Incorrect. Backtrack rewinds the DB to a specific time without creating a new cluster, but PITR is the standard feature for any-point restoration.

q: What is the Aurora Backtrack feature?

opts.a: A way to create a read replica in another region
opts.b: A way to rewind the database to a specific point in time without creating a new cluster
opts.c: A way to take manual snapshots
opts.d: A way to enable encryption on existing clusters

exp.a: Incorrect. Cross-region replicas are part of Global Database, not Backtrack.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora Backtrack allows you to rewind the DB cluster to a specific point in time without restoring from a backup or creating a new cluster.
exp.c: Incorrect. Manual snapshots are a separate feature from Backtrack.
exp.d: Incorrect. Encryption management is separate from the Backtrack feature.

q: What is the maximum backtrack window for Aurora Backtrack?

exp.a: Incorrect. The maximum backtrack window is 72 hours, not 24 hours.
exp.b: Incorrect. The maximum is 72 hours, not 48 hours.
exp.c: Correct. Aurora Backtrack supports a maximum backtrack window of 72 hours (3 days).
exp.d: Incorrect. 7 days exceeds the maximum backtrack window of 72 hours.

q: Which Aurora compatibility mode supports the Backtrack feature?

opts.c: Both Aurora MySQL and Aurora PostgreSQL
opts.d: Neither; it requires a special edition

exp.a: Incorrect. Backtrack is currently supported only for Aurora MySQL, not PostgreSQL.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora Backtrack is currently available only for Aurora MySQL-compatible edition.
exp.c: Incorrect. Backtrack is not available for Aurora PostgreSQL at this time.
exp.d: Incorrect. Backtrack is available for Aurora MySQL without any special edition.

q: What does Aurora Cloning use to create a copy of the database efficiently?

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora Cloning does not perform a full data copy initially.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora Cloning uses a copy-on-write protocol, creating a clone almost instantly without duplicating all data upfront.
exp.c: Incorrect. Cloning is different from snapshot restore; it uses copy-on-write and is much faster.
exp.d: Incorrect. Logical replication is a different mechanism; cloning uses copy-on-write.

q: What encryption standard does Amazon Aurora use for encrypting data at rest?

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora uses AES-256, not AES-128.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora encrypts data at rest using AES-256 encryption via AWS KMS.
exp.c: Incorrect. RSA-2048 is used for key exchange, not for data-at-rest encryption in Aurora.
exp.d: Incorrect. 3DES is an older standard not used by Aurora.

q: Which AWS service does Aurora use to manage encryption keys?

exp.a: Incorrect. While CloudHSM can be used, Aurora natively integrates with AWS KMS for encryption key management.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora uses AWS KMS to manage encryption keys for data at rest.
exp.c: Incorrect. Secrets Manager manages credentials, not Aurora encryption keys.
exp.d: Incorrect. Certificate Manager manages SSL/TLS certificates, not database encryption keys.

q: Can you enable encryption on an existing unencrypted Aurora cluster directly?

opts.a: Yes, you can enable encryption at any time
opts.b: No, you must create an encrypted snapshot and restore from it
opts.c: Yes, but only during a maintenance window
opts.d: No, encryption can never be added after creation

exp.a: Incorrect. You cannot enable encryption directly on an existing unencrypted Aurora cluster.
exp.b: Correct. To encrypt an existing unencrypted cluster, you must take a snapshot, copy it with encryption enabled, and restore from the encrypted snapshot.
exp.c: Incorrect. Encryption cannot be toggled on during a maintenance window.
exp.d: Incorrect. While you can't enable it directly, you can achieve encryption by the snapshot/restore method.

q: What protocol does Aurora use to encrypt data in transit?

exp.a: Incorrect. SSH is used for server access, not database connection encryption.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora supports SSL/TLS encryption for data in transit between the application and the database.
exp.c: Incorrect. IPSec is for VPN tunnels, not Aurora database connections.
exp.d: Incorrect. HTTPS is for web traffic; Aurora uses SSL/TLS for database connections.

q: Which authentication method allows Aurora to use IAM roles and policies for database access?

exp.a: Incorrect. Standard username/password is the traditional method, not IAM-based.
exp.b: Correct. IAM Database Authentication allows you to use IAM roles and policies to manage database access without passwords.
exp.c: Incorrect. LDAP is for directory-based authentication, not IAM integration.
exp.d: Incorrect. While Aurora PostgreSQL supports Kerberos, the question asks about IAM-based access.

q: What is an Aurora DB cluster?

opts.b: A collection of DB instances and a shared cluster storage volume
opts.d: A collection of S3 buckets storing database files

exp.a: Incorrect. An Aurora cluster is more than a single instance; it includes one or more instances.
exp.b: Correct. An Aurora DB cluster consists of one or more DB instances and a cluster volume that manages the data for those instances.
exp.c: Incorrect. DynamoDB tables are not part of an Aurora cluster.
exp.d: Incorrect. Aurora uses its own cluster storage, not S3 buckets for primary data.

q: What is the primary instance in an Aurora cluster responsible for?

exp.a: Incorrect. The primary instance handles write operations in addition to reads.
exp.b: Correct. The primary instance supports both read and write operations and is the only instance that can perform writes.
exp.c: Incorrect. Backups are handled by the storage layer automatically.
exp.d: Incorrect. Monitoring is done by CloudWatch, not exclusively the primary instance.

q: What happens when the primary instance in an Aurora cluster fails?

opts.b: An Aurora Replica is automatically promoted to primary
opts.c: A new instance must be manually created

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora is designed for high availability and will failover automatically.
exp.b: Correct. When the primary fails, Aurora automatically promotes an existing replica to become the new primary instance.
exp.c: Incorrect. If no replica exists, Aurora will create a new primary, but with replicas the failover is automatic.
exp.d: Incorrect. Data is stored in the shared cluster volume and is not lost during failover.

q: What is the Aurora Custom Endpoint used for?

opts.b: Routing connections to a specific subset of instances based on workload

exp.a: Incorrect. The reader endpoint distributes across all replicas; custom endpoints target specific subsets.
exp.b: Correct. Custom endpoints allow you to route connections to a specific group of instances for different workloads (e.g., analytics on larger instances).
exp.c: Incorrect. Encryption is handled by SSL/TLS, not custom endpoints.
exp.d: Incorrect. Custom endpoints work within a cluster, not specifically for cross-region.

q: Which AWS service can be used to monitor Aurora performance metrics?

exp.a: Incorrect. CloudTrail logs API calls, not performance metrics.
exp.b: Correct. Amazon CloudWatch is used to monitor Aurora performance metrics like CPU, memory, connections, and more.
exp.c: Incorrect. AWS Config tracks resource configuration changes, not performance metrics.
exp.d: Incorrect. AWS Inspector is for security vulnerability assessment, not database monitoring.

q: What Aurora feature provides detailed database performance insights using machine learning?

exp.a: Incorrect. Enhanced Monitoring provides OS-level metrics, not ML-based performance analysis.
exp.b: Correct. Performance Insights provides a dashboard to analyze database load and identify performance bottlenecks.
exp.c: Incorrect. CloudWatch Logs stores log data but doesn't provide ML-based performance insights.
exp.d: Incorrect. X-Ray is for application tracing, not database performance analysis.

q: What is the minimum storage that Aurora allocates when you create a new cluster?

opts.d: No minimum; it starts at actual data size

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora starts with a minimum of 10 GB.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora storage starts at 10 GB and automatically grows in 10 GB increments up to 128 TB.
exp.c: Incorrect. The minimum is 10 GB, not 20 GB.
exp.d: Incorrect. Aurora allocates a minimum of 10 GB regardless of actual data size.

q: Which pricing model is available for Aurora that allows you to pay per second of usage?

exp.a: Incorrect. On-Demand charges per hour for provisioned instances.
exp.b: Incorrect. Reserved Instances provide a discount for committed usage, not per-second billing.
exp.c: Correct. Aurora Serverless charges per second for the database capacity used, making it truly pay-per-use.
exp.d: Incorrect. Spot Instances are not available for Aurora.

q: Can you use Reserved Instances with Amazon Aurora provisioned?

opts.a: No, only On-Demand pricing is available
opts.b: Yes, you can purchase Aurora Reserved Instances for cost savings

exp.b: Correct. You can purchase Aurora Reserved Instances with 1-year or 3-year terms for significant cost savings.
exp.c: Incorrect. Reserved Instances are available for both Aurora MySQL and PostgreSQL.
exp.d: Incorrect. Reserved Instances apply to both Aurora MySQL and PostgreSQL.

q: What is the purpose of Aurora Auto Scaling?

opts.b: To automatically add or remove Aurora Replicas based on demand
opts.c: To automatically increase the instance class size
opts.d: To automatically replicate data across regions

exp.a: Incorrect. Storage scaling is automatic by default; Auto Scaling refers to compute replicas.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora Auto Scaling dynamically adds or removes Aurora Replicas in response to changes in connectivity or workload.
exp.c: Incorrect. Vertical scaling (instance class) is not handled by Aurora Auto Scaling.
exp.d: Incorrect. Cross-region replication is handled by Global Database, not Auto Scaling.

q: What is Aurora Multi-Master?

opts.a: A feature that allows read replicas in multiple regions
opts.b: A feature that allows multiple DB instances to perform both read and write operations
opts.c: A feature for automated backups to multiple locations
opts.d: A feature that provides multiple reader endpoints

exp.c: Incorrect. Backup to multiple locations is handled automatically, not by Multi-Master.
exp.d: Incorrect. Multiple reader endpoints are custom endpoints; Multi-Master is about write scaling.

q: What is the maximum number of instances in an Aurora Multi-Master cluster?

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora Multi-Master initially supported 2, but can support up to 4 writer instances.
exp.b: Correct. Aurora Multi-Master supports up to 4 DB instances that can all process write operations.
exp.c: Incorrect. The maximum for Multi-Master is 4 instances.
exp.d: Incorrect. 15 is the maximum for read replicas in a standard Aurora cluster, not Multi-Master.

q: Which feature of Aurora allows you to run SQL queries directly against data stored in Amazon S3?

opts.c: Aurora with S3 integration (querying S3 data via Aurora)

exp.b: Incorrect. Aurora ML integrates with SageMaker and Comprehend, not S3 queries.
exp.c: Correct. Aurora allows you to query data in S3 directly using the aws_s3 extension (PostgreSQL) or LOAD DATA FROM S3 (MySQL).

q: Which AWS ML services can Aurora Machine Learning integrate with natively?

exp.a: Correct. Aurora Machine Learning natively integrates with Amazon SageMaker and Amazon Comprehend to run ML predictions via SQL.
exp.b: Incorrect. Rekognition and Polly are not natively integrated with Aurora ML.

opts.b: Distributing query processing across the storage layer for faster analytical queries

exp.b: Correct. Aurora Parallel Query pushes down and distributes query processing across the Aurora storage layer, speeding up analytical queries.
exp.c: Incorrect. Cross-region replication is handled by Global Database, not Parallel Query.
exp.d: Incorrect. Cloning is a separate feature from Parallel Query.

q: What type of database is Amazon Aurora classified as?

q: How does Aurora handle database patching and maintenance?

opts.a: Users must manually apply all patches

opts.d: Patching is not needed for Aurora

q: What is the Aurora Serverless v2 minimum capacity?

q: What is the maximum capacity for Aurora Serverless v2?

exp.b: Correct. Aurora Serverless v2 can scale up to a maximum of 128 ACUs.
exp.c: Incorrect. The maximum is 128 ACUs, not 256.
exp.d: Incorrect. The maximum is 128 ACUs, not 512.

q: Which VPC component is required to deploy Amazon Aurora?

opts.b: DB Subnet Group (with subnets in at least 2 AZs)

q: What is the maximum size of an Aurora database snapshot?

opts.a: Limited to the current database size

q: Which of the following is NOT a valid Aurora instance class family?

q: What is the SLA (Service Level Agreement) uptime commitment for Amazon Aurora?

exp.a: Incorrect. Aurora's SLA is higher than 99.9%.
exp.b: Incorrect. Aurora offers a higher SLA than 99.95%.
exp.c: Correct. Amazon Aurora offers an SLA of 99.99% availability.
exp.d: Incorrect. While Aurora is designed for high availability, the SLA commitment is 99.99%, not 99.999%.

q: How does Aurora handle storage-level failures?

opts.b: Aurora automatically detects and repairs storage failures using data from the other copies
opts.c: The entire cluster must be restarted
opts.d: A support ticket must be raised

exp.b: Correct. Aurora continuously monitors disk health and automatically repairs any failures using data from the remaining copies.

exp.d: Incorrect. No support ticket is needed; the self-healing mechanism handles it automatically.

q: What is the Aurora Data API used for?

opts.a: Streaming data into Aurora in real time
opts.b: Accessing Aurora Serverless via HTTP-based API calls without persistent database connections

exp.a: Incorrect. Streaming data would use services like Kinesis, not the Data API.
exp.b: Correct. The Aurora Data API allows you to run SQL queries through HTTP-based API calls, useful for serverless applications that don't maintain persistent connections.
exp.c: Incorrect. DMS (Database Migration Service) handles migrations, not the Data API.
